1.q: A programme manager claims a long-running internal reporting initiative is a project because it required initial funding approval and produced a new dashboard. The team now continuously updates reports and adds minor features every month. Which judgement best aligns with the APM definition of a project?
o: It is a project because it involves stakeholders and delivers organisational value
It remains a project because it produces outputs that can be enhanced over time
It is no longer a project because the work has transitioned into ongoing operational activity
It is a project only if the dashboard continues to evolve in response to stakeholder feedback
It remains a project because it originally had a defined start and funding approval
1.w: Once work becomes continuous and repetitive, it shifts from temporary endeavour to BAU, even if it originated as a project.

n.0: Value delivery alone does not distinguish projects from BAU.
n.1: Ongoing enhancement does not maintain project status; repetition indicates BAU.
n.3: Evolution alone does not define a project; temporariness is key.
n.4: Historical characteristics do not define current classification.

1.q: A programme board is deciding whether to adopt an extended life cycle for an initiative whose value will only become apparent once the delivered capability is in use. The sponsor wants to understand what advantages the extension brings. Which TWO benefits are most associated with using an extended life cycle?
o: Elimination of feedback
Verification of outcomes
Improved value realisation
Fixed scope definition
Reduced governance
1.w: Extended life cycles ensure outcomes and value are realised.

1.q: A delivery team proposes three options to recover schedule slippage. The project board chooses the cheapest option without considering risk or benefit impact. What has most clearly failed?
o: Team motivation
Procurement strategy
Decision quality within governance
Technical configuration control
Resource planning
1.w: Governance decisions should consider balanced criteria, not cost alone.

1.q: On a delivery schedule, an activity that lies on the critical path is finished ahead of its planned finish date, and no other constraints currently limit the work that follows. The project manager is assessing what this means for the timeline. What is the most likely impact?
o: Other dependent activities will be delayed as a result
Float will increase evenly across all of the remaining activities
The critical path through the network will be eliminated
The project will automatically finish ahead of its deadline
The project end date may improve if no other constraints exist
1.w: Early completion of critical activities can reduce overall duration if no other constraints limit progress.

1.q: A project delivers a new CRM system, but user adoption remains low and sales performance does not improve. Which statement best reflects the distinction being demonstrated?
o: The project delivered outcomes but lacked defined outputs
The project failed because it did not deliver its output
The project delivered outputs but failed to realise outcomes
The project cannot be assessed without stakeholder feedback
The project succeeded because outputs were delivered within scope
1.w: The CRM system is an output, but improved sales is the intended outcome, which was not achieved.

n.1: The output was delivered; failure relates to outcomes.
n.3: The distinction is clear without further input.
n.4: Success requires more than output delivery.

1.q: A project has delivered its outputs and the team is keen to close down immediately without continuing into an extended life cycle. The assurance reviewer warns the sponsor about what could be lost by stopping at handover. Which TWO risks arise if an extended life cycle is not used?
o: Improved predictability
Unrealised benefits
Lack of outcome verification
Reduced stakeholder engagement
Faster closure
1.w: Without extension, benefits may not be realised or verified.

n.4: Closure speed is not the main issue.

1.q: A project manager escalates a supplier dispute to the sponsor because it threatens delivery tolerances. The sponsor criticises the escalation as unnecessary detail. What is the best assessment?
o: The sponsor is correct because supplier issues are never governance matters
The team should resolve all supplier issues without escalation
The project manager acted appropriately because tolerances were threatened
The dispute should only be reported after project closure
Escalation should be avoided unless costs have already been incurred
1.w: Issues threatening tolerances should be escalated so governance roles can make or support required decisions.

1.q: A two-day delay occurs on an activity shown as critical. No resources were added, no activities were overlapped and the logic was not changed, yet the forecast completion date is unaffected. What is the most plausible explanation?
o: Dependencies on the activity were removed
The activity was wrongly identified as critical
Critical activities always carry some float
Delays under a week never affect the end date
Extra resources were added to recover the lost time
1.w: Critical activities have zero total float, so any delay to them delays the end date. As nothing was done to recover the time, the activity must have had float, meaning it was not truly critical.

n.0: The scenario states the logic was not changed.
n.2: Activities on the critical path have zero total float by definition.
n.3: Any delay to a genuinely critical activity delays completion, however short.
n.4: The scenario states no resources were added, so crashing did not recover the time.

1.q: A project team is tasked with implementing a process used successfully in another division with minimal changes. Which factor most challenges whether this work should be considered a project?
o: The existence of predefined deliverables
The need for formal governance approval
The requirement to deliver within a set timeframe
The presence of stakeholders across divisions
The lack of uniqueness in the work being performed
1.w: Projects require uniqueness; replicating standard processes reduces this characteristic.

n.0: Deliverables exist in both projects and BAU.
n.2: Time constraints alone do not define a project.
n.3: Stakeholders are present in both contexts.

1.q: A sponsor is selecting a life-cycle approach for an initiative whose success will depend on how the delivered capability performs once it is in everyday use, not merely on completing the outputs. Which TWO situations justify adopting an extended life cycle?
o: No stakeholder involvement
Immediate project closure required
Need to track outcomes
Benefits realised over time
Fixed outputs only
1.w: Extended life cycles suit projects where benefits emerge over time.

n.4: Outputs alone do not justify extension.

1.q: A governance group approves a project but does not define decision rights, tolerance limits or escalation thresholds. What is the most likely consequence?
o: The project will need less reporting
Stakeholder engagement will automatically improve
The project manager will have clearer autonomy
Decisions will become inconsistent and accountability unclear
The project board will be unnecessary
1.w: Without decision rights and escalation thresholds, governance becomes inconsistent and accountability weakens.

1.q: A project manager is examining a network diagram and needs to work out which activities lie on the critical path by applying the correct defining test. She wants to reason from the underlying rule rather than a general impression. Which situation most accurately indicates that an activity is on the critical path?
o: It is the most complex task
It requires the most resources
It is the first activity in the schedule
It has the longest duration in the project
It has zero float and directly impacts project completion
1.w: Critical path activities have zero float and directly affect project duration.

1.q: A manager describes a project as ‘any work that has a start and end date’. What is the most accurate critique of this statement?
o: It ignores the need to engage and involve stakeholders
It overlooks the governance structures that all projects require
It overemphasises delivering outputs rather than achieving useful outcomes
It incorrectly assumes that all BAU work is continuous
It fails to recognise that temporary work must also be unique
1.w: Temporariness alone is insufficient; projects must also be unique.

n.0: Stakeholders are not the defining factor.
n.1: Governance is not part of the core definition.
n.2: Outputs vs outcomes is not the central issue.

1.q: A project governance board requests assurance reports from an independent reviewer. What is the main purpose of this oversight activity?
o: To take over the project manager's delivery responsibilities
To approve each operational decision made during delivery
To provide confidence that the project is controlled and aligned
To transfer accountability from the sponsor to the reviewer
To remove the need for any further stakeholder consultation
1.w: Assurance gives governance bodies confidence that delivery, risks and controls remain appropriate.

1.q: When monitoring progress, a project manager reviews only the activities on the critical path and pays no attention to those carrying small amounts of float. A colleague warns him that this narrow focus is hazardous. What risk does concentrating solely on the critical path create?
o: The project will finish early
The schedule will become inaccurate
Critical activities may be delayed
Non-critical activities may become critical without detection
Resources will be over-allocated
1.w: Ignoring near-critical activities risks them becoming critical due to unmonitored delays.

1.q: During project initiation, a sponsor emphasises that success will be measured by improved customer satisfaction rather than system deployment. What is this primarily highlighting?
o: Outputs should be deprioritised in favour of deliverables
Customer satisfaction is an operational metric only
Outputs and outcomes are interchangeable in project success
Outcomes are more significant than outputs in defining value
Projects should not focus on technical deliverables
1.w: Outcomes represent benefits and value, whereas outputs are deliverables.

n.1: Customer satisfaction can be a project outcome.

1.q: On a business-change project, the individual who represents the end users has been left out of governance decisions that set the priorities for accepting deliverables. The project manager is concerned about the consequences of this omission. What is the most likely risk that results?
o: The project manager will lose all delivery authority
The governance board will become too large
Decisions may not reflect user needs or acceptance criteria
The escalation process will become unnecessary
Supplier costs will automatically increase
1.w: Governance decisions need appropriate representation so user needs and acceptance priorities are considered.

1.q: A project manager is reviewing a schedule and wants to anticipate which type of change would shift the critical path and thereby alter the overall duration. She is weighing several possible adjustments to different activities. Which change is most likely to alter the critical path?
o: Adding resources to a non-critical task
Improving communication between stakeholders
Reordering independent tasks
Increasing the duration of a critical activity
Reducing the duration of a non-critical activity with float
1.w: Changes to critical activities directly affect the critical path and overall duration.

1.q: A house-building firm operates an estate where crews put up identical units, each to the same standardised design, method and sequence, week after week. Although every individual unit has its own start and finish, the work itself varies little from one to the next. How should this work most appropriately be classified?
o: BAU only if there are no external stakeholders
A project because each house produces a distinct output
A project because each house has a defined completion date
A hybrid of project and BAU due to repetition
BAU because the work lacks uniqueness despite being temporary per unit
1.w: Repetitive work with minimal variation is BAU, even if outputs are discrete.

n.1: Outputs alone do not define projects.
n.3: Classification depends on characteristics, not blending.

1.q: A sponsor wants to assure herself that the governance board is genuinely providing oversight rather than merely receiving reports. She is looking for the signs that oversight is working effectively across the project. Which TWO features indicate effective project governance oversight?
o: Avoiding escalation to preserve delivery speed
Delegating sponsor accountability to the project team
Regular review of alignment with business objectives
Approval of every minor team-level decision
Monitoring whether tolerances remain under control
1.w: Effective oversight checks strategic alignment and whether the project remains within agreed controls.

2.q: During a schedule review, the project manager notices that one activity in the network has been calculated with negative float. She needs to interpret correctly what this value is telling her about the project's position. What does negative float on this activity indicate?
o: The activity has no dependencies
The activity is ahead of schedule
The critical path has been shortened
The activity is delaying the project completion
The project is ahead of plan
2.w: Negative float indicates that the schedule is behind and the activity is impacting completion.

2.q: A digital transformation initiative is described as ‘ongoing, evolving, and continuously improving processes’. Why is this description problematic when defining it as a project?
o: It ignores the need for ongoing stakeholder engagement
It suggests a complete absence of governance arrangements
It provides no clarity on the defined project outputs
It conflicts with the temporary nature required for projects
It overstates the importance of long-term outcomes
2.w: Projects are temporary; ongoing evolution suggests BAU or programme activity.

n.0: Stakeholders are not the defining issue.
n.2: Outputs are not the main issue.

2.q: A newly appointed project manager is clarifying with the sponsor when matters should be raised to the governance board rather than handled within the team. He wants to recognise the circumstances that ought to prompt escalation. Which TWO situations should normally trigger escalation within project governance?
o: A routine task completed by the team
A planned meeting taking place as scheduled
A forecast breach of agreed tolerance
A decision needed beyond the project manager's delegated authority
A minor update to a team checklist
2.w: Escalation is appropriate when tolerances are threatened or decisions exceed delegated authority.

2.q: A sponsor has asked the project manager to bring the planned completion date forward and is pressing for the most effective scheduling response. The manager is deciding where to direct compression effort within the network. Which action would most effectively reduce the overall project duration?
o: Increasing the schedule contingency allowance
Adding extra float into the schedule
Extending the durations of critical activities
Reducing the duration of critical activities
Shortening the duration of non-critical activities
2.w: Only reducing critical path durations directly shortens the overall project timeline.

2.q: A team delivers a software tool exactly as specified, but users adapt it in unexpected ways to generate additional benefits. What does this illustrate?
o: Outcomes may differ from intended outputs
Outputs should not be defined at project start
Outcomes emerge from how outputs are used
Outputs can directly control outcomes
Outputs and outcomes are independent and unrelated
2.w: Outcomes depend on how outputs are applied in practice.

n.0: Outcomes do not differ from outputs; they are distinct.
n.3: Outputs do not fully control outcomes.

2.q: A newly formed governance board wants its decision-making to be consistent and defensible, so that similar requests are handled the same way each time rather than case by case. The sponsor asks what the framework must set out. Which TWO elements should a governance decision framework normally clarify?
o: Authority required for different decision types
Membership of each delivery team
Technical method to be used for each work package
Named owners for each risk in the risk register
Criteria for comparing options
2.w: A decision framework makes decisions consistent and defensible by setting out the criteria used to compare options and the level of authority needed for each type of decision, so similar requests are judged the same way and taken at the right level.

n.1: Team membership is set out in the organisation structure and resource plans; it does not tell the board how to make or authorise decisions.
n.2: Technical methods are a delivery matter for the team and specialists, not something a governance decision framework prescribes.
n.3: Risk owners are recorded in the risk register as part of risk management; they do not define how the board compares options or who may decide.

2.q: An assessor asks a project manager to explain precisely what makes an activity 'critical' within a network diagram. The manager must set out its true defining attributes rather than a loose impression of importance. Which TWO characteristics define a critical activity?
o: Highest cost
Longest duration
Requires specialist resources
Direct impact on project completion
Zero float
2.w: Critical activities have zero float and directly influence completion.

2.q: A finance director is reviewing several strands of work across the organisation to decide which should be governed as a project. She wants the one that is genuinely temporary, unique and produces a defined change rather than sustaining existing operations. Which of the following most clearly represents a project?
o: Implementing a new enterprise resource planning system
Updating employee records in HR systems
Continuous system maintenance and patching
Processing daily customer orders
Monthly financial reporting using standard templates
2.w: ERP implementation is unique and temporary, aligning with project definition.

2.q: An assurance reviewer has found that a portfolio's governance oversight is applied only intermittently and superficially. She is preparing to explain to the sponsor the dangers this creates for projects running beneath it. Which TWO risks are created by weak governance oversight?
o: Reduced need for assurance
Late identification of major issues
Strategic drift from business objectives
Clearer escalation thresholds
Improved decision consistency
2.w: Weak oversight can allow projects to drift and issues to surface too late.

2.q: A project manager has been building a schedule while taking no account of the float on various activities as he plans and sequences the work. An assurance reviewer cautions that this oversight carries consequences. Which TWO risks are associated with ignoring float in scheduling decisions?
o: Improved flexibility
Reduced project complexity
Unexpected delays affecting the critical path
Misallocation of resources
Shortened timelines
2.w: Ignoring float can lead to resource misallocation and delays impacting critical activities.

2.q: During an induction session, a sponsor asks new team members to distinguish undertakings that qualify as projects from routine operational work. She wants them to name the defining attributes set out in APM guidance. Which TWO characteristics are essential to defining a piece of work as a project?
o: Continuous improvement
Temporary nature
Ongoing operational support
Repetitive execution
Uniqueness of deliverables
2.w: Projects are temporary and unique endeavours.

2.q: Following an incident where a serious problem was raised too late and to the wrong manager, a sponsor wants to make escalation more disciplined on future projects. She asks which measures would achieve this. Which TWO actions would strengthen escalation discipline in a project?
o: Encourage informal escalation to any senior manager
Clarify who has authority to approve exceptions
Define tolerance thresholds at the start
Remove the project manager from decision-making
Delay reporting until a problem is irreversible
2.w: Clear tolerances and approval authority make escalation controlled and timely.

2.q: Midway through delivery, a project manager wants to anticipate which developments could cause the critical path to shift to a different sequence of activities. He is considering several things that might happen across the network. Which TWO scenarios could cause a change in the critical path?
o: Adding contingency to the schedule
Reducing float on non-critical tasks
Improving team communication
Increasing duration of critical activities
Delays in near-critical activities
2.w: Changes to critical or near-critical activities can shift the critical path.

2.q: A project manager is briefing an apprentice on how float behaves within a schedule. She wants the apprentice to retain only the statements that are accurate and to set aside the misconceptions. Which TWO statements about float are correct?
o: Float exists only on critical activities
Float allows flexibility in scheduling
Float is fixed throughout the project
Float eliminates uncertainty
Float can absorb delays without affecting completion
2.w: Float provides flexibility and can absorb delays without affecting completion.

2.q: A review of a project's plan finds that its milestones have been described vaguely, with no clear criteria for when each is reached. The sponsor asks what problems such loosely defined milestones are likely to cause. Which TWO risks arise from poorly defined milestones?
o: Faster reporting cycles
Improved stakeholder clarity
Misaligned decision points
Reduced project complexity
Ambiguous progress measurement
2.w: Poor definition leads to unclear progress and ineffective decision-making.

2.q: While building the business case for a digital transformation programme, the project sponsor asks the team to document the internal capabilities and resources that set the organisation apart from its rivals and give it a competitive edge. In a SWOT analysis, these internal positive attributes are known as what?
o: Weaknesses
Strengths
Opportunities
Threats
Ambiguity
2.w: Strengths are internal positive attributes of the organisation.

2.q: Which TWO risks arise from poor hybrid implementation?
o: Better alignment
Improved clarity
Confusion
Reduced flexibility
Loss of control
2.w: Poor hybrid use leads to confusion and reduced control.

2.q: A time-critical project needs decisions made quickly, but it is being delivered within a weak matrix where authority sits largely with the functional departments. The project manager is concerned about how this will affect progress. What is the most likely impact?
o: No impact on decision-making speed
Increased autonomy for project teams
Delays caused by reliance on functional approval
Faster approvals due to shared authority
Elimination of governance processes
2.w: Weak matrices require functional approvals, slowing decisions.

2.q: A project manager wants to ensure the benefits promised at the outset still support the organisation's direction as the project progresses. Which two elements must be aligned to ensure benefits remain relevant throughout the project?
o: Project charter and issue log
Benefit metrics and organisational strategy
Scope statement and resource calendar
Risk appetite and communication plan
Quality management plan and test cases
2.w: Aligning metrics with strategy ensures benefits support corporate goals.

n.0: Charter and issue log are unrelated.
n.2: Scope and resources relate to execution.
n.3: Risk and communication are separate functions.
n.4: Quality plan and test cases focus on deliverables.

2.q: Which document outlines project procurement requirements for suppliers?
o: Stakeholder register
Quality management plan
Statement of Work (SOW)
Communications matrix
Risk register
2.w: The Statement of Work details objectives, deliverables, and requirements for procurement.

n.0: The stakeholder register lists stakeholders and roles.
n.1: Quality plans focus on standards, not procurement.
n.3: The communications matrix maps information flows.
n.4: The risk register logs project risks.
